Our 8 year old noticed the truck “breathes” around 45 mph. I spent two weeks working out why.

A dad, a napkin, and a question from the back seat that changed his weekend.

The truck
2016 Silverado 15005.3L V884,000 milesSchool run and Sunday truck
From the back seat“Dad, why does the truck breathe?”

It’s a 2016 Silverado 1500 with the 5.3 and 84,000 miles. It takes my son to school, and to his grandmother’s on Sundays.

From the back seat, juice box in hand, Mason (he’s 8) asked why the truck breathes. “It goes in and out,” he said. “Like when I hold my breath.”

I eased off the gas around 45 and there it was: a soft change in the engine note, like the truck took a breath and let it go.

Two weeks of forum reading and one cousin who works on trucks later, my friend Rick sketched it out on a napkin.

Mason studied it and asked, “Doesn’t a light switch break if you flip it too much?”

An 8 year old had just said what three adults had been circling for two weeks.

I’d like to say I was proud of finding the fix. Mostly I felt a little embarrassed. He noticed before I did. I’d driven that truck for years and never wondered what the engine does when I’m not asking it for anything.

I plugged the module in that weekend. On the drive to his grandmother’s, Mason went quiet for a mile, then said the thing I’ve been repeating since.

Dad. It stopped breathing.Mason, age 8, after the install

If you drive a GM truck or SUV with a V6 or V8, that same little breath is in your engine. Most of us never hear it. A kid in a back seat did.

Try it yourself: the 45 mph test

You can feel the system switching on many GM V8 trucks. Here’s how.

  • Find a flat, quiet road and settle in at a steady 40 to 55 mph.
  • Hold speed with very little pedal. Radio off, windows up.
  • Listen and feel for a soft change in the engine note, sometimes with a faint vibration, as the cylinders switch.
  • Check the driver display. On some trims it shows a V4 or ECO indicator when it happens.

Many drivers never notice it, and not noticing it doesn’t mean anything is wrong. It’s just a way to see the system working.

What Mason was hearing

Here’s the answer to his question, in plain English.

Half the engine takes a break

While you cruise at a steady speed, GM’s Active Fuel Management (AFM, called DFM on newer trucks) shuts off some of the cylinders to save a little fuel.

A tiny pin does the switching

The lifters on those cylinders carry a small locking pin. It locks or releases every time the system switches, hundreds of times on a normal drive.

Pins wear. Sometimes they let go

When one gives out, the lifter can collapse and start grinding into the camshaft. Most of these engines get through it. Some don’t, and nobody can tell you ahead of time which ones.

Example shown for a V8. V6 versions work the same way with fewer cylinders.

That’s the “breath” Mason felt: cylinders switching off, and then back on.

Questions people ask first

Can I feel the difference myself?

On many trucks you can feel the system switching around 40 to 55 mph at light throttle. After installing, some drivers report a steadier feel. Results vary.

How hard is the install?

Plug it into the OBD2 port under the dash, the same port a mechanic uses to read codes. No tools. It takes seconds.

Will it fit my truck?

Use the fitment checker on this page. It runs on the same compatibility list as the store and covers Silverado, Sierra, Tahoe, Yukon, Suburban, Escalade and more, with V6 and V8 engines.

Does it change or reprogram my truck?

No. It doesn’t touch the truck’s computer (the ECU) and nothing is written to your truck. Pull it out and the truck reads factory.

Will my fuel economy change?

It can. AFM exists to save GM a little fuel, roughly 1 to 2 MPG. Keeping every cylinder firing can give some of that back. Reviewers report little or no change, but your driving will decide.

Will it void my warranty?

It’s fully removable and leaves nothing behind, so many owners simply unplug it before a dealer visit. Every dealer and warranty is different, so if this matters to you, check yours.

Will it repair a lifter that’s already worn?

No. Nothing plugged into a port can repair worn parts. If your truck is ticking, shuddering or losing power right now, have it looked at first. FullForce is for stopping the switching from continuing, not for undoing damage.
